claims.text: NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center advisory (11 PM HST, 15 August 2026): Hurricane Lala had maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 988 mb, located near latitude 19.6N, longitude 157.0W, about 65 miles west of Kailua-Kona and 130 miles south-southeast of Honolulu, moving northwest at 15 mph with gradual weakening expected Sunday. Forecast rainfall totals were 4-8 inches for the Big Island and windward Maui with a storm-total maximum of 30-35 inches over windward Hawaii Island, and 4-6 inches (maximum 8 inches) for the remaining islands, with 1-3 feet of storm surge; the advisory warned these amounts 'will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.'

GDACS tropical cyclone report for ONE-C-26/Lala (episode 23, reporting window 12 Aug 2026 15:00 UTC - 18 Aug 2026 03:00 UTC): overall Green alert (low humanitarian impact) with maximum sustained winds of 148 km/h (Category 1) and an affected population of approximately 10,000 people in Category 1 or higher wind zones, both consistent with the prior report; the primary GDACS event assessment records no deaths or damage figures (a separate media-headlines module on the same page cites third-party news reports of one storm-related death and up to ~111,000 customers without power on Hawaii Island, which are not GDACS's own assessed figures).

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 28 (11 PM HST, 18 August 2026): Hurricane Lala re-intensified to a Category 4 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 130 mph (215 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 947 mb, located near 20.9N 169.7W, about 310 miles south of Maro Reef and 450 miles southeast of Lisianski Island, moving northwest at 9 mph. A Hurricane Warning is in effect for the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski Island to Maro Reef, and a Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for the Monument east of Maro Reef to French Frigate Shoals -- the first coastal watches/warnings posted since Lala passed the main Hawaiian Islands. Some gradual weakening is anticipated during the next few days, but Lala is expected to remain a hurricane. GDACS's tropical cyclone report (reporting window 12-19 August 2026) records the storm at Category 4 strength (213 km/h), an unchanged affected-population estimate of about 10,000 people, and continued Green/low-impact status, with no deaths or damage in GDACS's own assessment. The Office of the Governor of Hawaii and the County of Hawaii both returned HTTP 403 Forbidden on every page fetched again today, so no allowlisted government source could be reached to confirm a death toll, injury count, power-outage figure, or damage total.

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 32 (11 PM HST, 19 August 2026): Hurricane Lala has weakened to a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 963 mb, located near 23.5N 171.9W, about 150 miles southwest of Maro Reef and 225 miles southeast of Lisianski Island, moving north-northwest at 9 mph. A Hurricane Warning remains in effect for the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski Island to Maro Reef, and a Tropical Storm Warning remains in effect for the Monument east of Maro Reef to French Frigate Shoals -- no watches or warnings for the main Hawaiian Islands. Lala is forecast to remain a hurricane through the weekend as gradual weakening continues.

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 36 (11 PM HST, 20 August 2026): Hurricane Lala remained a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (155 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 971 mb, located near 26.6N 171.7W, about 115 miles northwest of Maro Reef and 145 miles northeast of Lisianski Island, moving north-northeast at 9 mph. A Hurricane Warning remained in effect for the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski Island to Maro Reef, and a Tropical Storm Warning remained in effect east of Maro Reef to French Frigate Shoals; no watches or warnings were in effect for the main Hawaiian Islands. Lala was forecast to remain a hurricane through Saturday with gradual weakening thereafter.

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 40 (11 PM HST, 21 August 2026): Hurricane Lala had maximum sustained winds of 85 mph (140 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 976 mb, located near 30.3N 172.0W, about 300 miles northeast of Pearl and Hermes Atoll, moving northwest at 14 mph. 'There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.' Gradual weakening is forecast during the next several days, and Lala's winds could decrease below hurricane force by early Sunday (23 August).

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 44 (11 PM HST, 22 August 2026): Lala has weakened to a tropical storm with maximum sustained winds of 70 mph (110 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 984 mb, located near 32.0N 173.7W, about 335 miles (540 km) north-northeast of Pearl and Hermes Atoll, moving northwest. "There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect." Gradual weakening is forecast to continue during the next several days.

Emergency Proclamation Relating to Tropical Storm Lala, signed 14 August 2026 by C. Kimo Alameda, Ph.D., Mayor of the County of Hawaiʻi, under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 127A, declaring a local state of emergency for Hawaiʻi County citing NWS forecasts of winds of 74-110 mph, rainfall of 8-12 inches (10-15 inches over windward areas), storm surge of 1-3 feet, and surf heights of 15-20 feet, with potential for 'considerable damage, downed trees and power lines, and power and communications disruptions.'

claims.source_name: Office of the Governor of Hawaiʻi
claims.text: Governor Josh Green signed a statewide emergency proclamation on 13 August 2026 ahead of Tropical Storm Lala, mobilizing state agency personnel, equipment and resources; the Hawaiʻi National Guard was prepared to support response efforts. A follow-up state update (16 August) reports approximately 180 Hawaiʻi National Guard personnel positioned statewide, including a 41-member Task Force Hawaiʻi and a 19-member Task Force Maui, and confirms the Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation closed Hilo International Airport (ITO) and Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport (KOA) at 2 p.m., with Hawaiʻi Island and Maui County commercial ports also closed to all terminal, facility and vessel operations absent US Coast Guard approval.

GDACS tracked the storm as Central Pacific tropical cyclone ONE-C-26, active 12-16 August 2026, rating it a Green alert (low humanitarian impact) with maximum sustained winds of 130 km/h (Category 1), an estimated 10,000 people affected by Category 1 or higher wind speeds, a maximum storm surge of 0.2 m, and 'low' vulnerability assessed for the United States.

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 20 (11 PM HST, 16 August 2026): Tropical Storm Lala located near 20.7N 162.6W, about 305 miles west of Honolulu and 225 miles west-southwest of Lihue, with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 997 mb, moving westward at 13 mph. 'There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.' Lala is forecast to become a hurricane again by Wednesday while continuing to move westward away from the main Hawaiian Islands.

County of Hawaiʻi update (posted 16 August 2026, 7:37 PM): all non-emergency County operations suspended Monday, 17 August, following Hurricane Lala's impact on the island; 'record-breaking' power outages reported (no specific figure given), multiple road closures documented on the County's Hazard Impact Map, 43 people sheltering at two emergency shelters (Nāʻālehu Elementary School and Robert N. Herkes Gym), search-and-rescue operations ongoing in Nāʻālehu, Waiʻōhinu and Pāhala, and an island-wide 'Essential Only' water-conservation request.

GDACS tropical cyclone report for ONE-C-26 (episode 20, reporting window 12 Aug 2026 15:00 UTC - 17 Aug 2026 09:00 UTC): overall Green alert (low humanitarian impact); maximum sustained winds 139 km/h (Category 1), up from 130 km/h in the prior report; affected population approximately 10,000 people in Category 1 or higher wind zones, unchanged.

County of Hawaiʻi flash-flooding update (16 August 2026, 1:07 AM): the County coordinated search-and-rescue operations in Nāʻālehu and Waiʻōhinu in Kaʻū after severe flash flooding cut off road access and inundated homes; National Guard high-water vehicles and a US Coast Guard helicopter assisted, and rescued residents were transported to Robert N. Herkes Gym in Pāhala and the Public Works base yard. Mayor Kimo Alameda: 'Our highest priority is the safety of our residents.'

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory Number 24 (11 PM HST, 17 August 2026): Hurricane Lala re-strengthened to a hurricane, located near 20.4N 166.1W, about 440 miles southeast of Maro Reef, with maximum sustained winds near 80 mph (130 km/h), higher gusts, and a minimum central pressure of 985 mb, moving toward the west near 10 mph. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles from the center and tropical-storm-force winds up to 90 miles. 'There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect,' though interests in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument were advised to monitor Lala's progress as watches would likely be needed early Tuesday. Additional strengthening was forecast during the next day or so, with the system expected to remain a hurricane for several days, moving west through Tuesday before turning northwest and then north by Thursday -- continuing to track away from the main Hawaiian Islands.

description: Hurricane Lala passed closest to Hawaii Island on 15-16 August 2026 as a Category 1 hurricane, with NOAA's 15 August advisory reporting 75 mph sustained winds about 65 miles west of Kailua-Kona and forecasting up to 30-35 inches of rain over windward Hawaii Island with life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Flash flooding cut off road access in Nāʻālehu and Waiʻōhinu in Kaʻū, prompting search-and-rescue operations; the County reported record-breaking power outages and 43 people in two emergency shelters, while the state -- which declared emergencies on 13 and 14 August and activated about 180 National Guard personnel -- closed Hilo and Kona airports and Hawaii Island and Maui County commercial ports. Lala tracked away from the main islands, re-intensified to Category 4 on 18 August, and has weakened steadily since: NOAA's Advisory 44 (11 PM HST, 22 August) put it at 70 mph sustained winds -- a tropical storm -- about 335 miles north-northeast of Pearl and Hermes Atoll, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect and continued gradual weakening forecast. No death toll, injury count or displacement total has been confirmed by an official state, county or NOAA source.

impact.summary: Lala's closest pass on 15-16 August 2026 brought severe flash flooding to Hawaii Island's Kaʻū district -- with search-and-rescue operations in Nāʻālehu, Waiʻōhinu and Pāhala -- record-breaking power outages, 43 people in two emergency shelters, airport and port closures, and an island-wide 'Essential Only' water-conservation request. No death toll, injury count, quantified power-outage figure or displacement total has been confirmed by an official state, county or NOAA source; GDACS's last assessment kept a Green/low-impact rating with about 10,000 people in Category 1-or-higher wind zones, while a media-headlines module on its report page cited third-party reports of one storm-related death and up to about 111,000 customers without power on Hawaii Island. As of NOAA's Advisory 44 (11 PM HST, 22 August), Lala had weakened to a tropical storm with 70 mph sustained winds and a 984 mb central pressure, about 335 miles north-northeast of Pearl and Hermes Atoll, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect and gradual weakening forecast to continue.

name: Hurricane Lala, Hawaii

updates.text: NOAA's Advisory 44 (11 PM HST, 22 August) reported Lala had weakened to a tropical storm -- 70 mph sustained winds, 984 mb central pressure -- about 335 miles north-northeast of Pearl and Hermes Atoll, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect and gradual weakening forecast to continue over the next several days.

NOAA's Advisory 40 (11 PM HST, 21 August) reported Lala at 85 mph sustained winds and a 976 mb central pressure, about 300 miles northeast of Pearl and Hermes Atoll, moving northwest at 14 mph with no coastal watches or warnings in effect; gradual weakening is forecast to take it below hurricane strength by early Sunday.

NOAA's Advisory 36 (11 PM HST, 20 August) reported Lala remained a Category 2 hurricane -- 100 mph sustained winds, 971 mb central pressure -- about 115 miles northwest of Maro Reef and 145 miles northeast of Lisianski Island, moving north-northeast at 9 mph and forecast to remain a hurricane through Saturday with gradual weakening thereafter.

NOAA's Advisory 32 (11 PM HST, 19 August) reported Lala had weakened to a Category 2 hurricane -- 105 mph sustained winds, 963 mb central pressure -- about 150 miles southwest of Maro Reef, continuing north-northwest away from the main Hawaiian Islands and forecast to remain a hurricane through the weekend.

NOAA's Advisory 28 (11 PM HST, 18 August) reported Lala had re-intensified into a Category 4 hurricane -- 130 mph sustained winds, 947 mb central pressure -- about 310 miles south of Maro Reef and moving northwest away from the main Hawaiian Islands. A Hurricane Warning and a Tropical Storm Warning were posted for the uninhabited Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument.

NOAA's Central Pacific Hurricane Center Advisory 24 (11 PM HST, 17 August) reported Lala had re-strengthened into a hurricane, with 80 mph sustained winds and a 985 mb central pressure about 440 miles southeast of Maro Reef, moving west away from the main Hawaiian Islands; no coastal watches or warnings were in effect.

The County of Hawaiʻi suspended all non-emergency operations for 17 August, reporting record-breaking power outages, multiple road closures, 43 people sheltering at Nāʻālehu Elementary School and Robert N. Herkes Gym, ongoing search-and-rescue in Nāʻālehu, Waiʻōhinu and Pāhala, and an island-wide 'Essential Only' water-conservation request.

NOAA Advisory 20 (11 PM HST, 16 August) downgraded Lala to a tropical storm with 60 mph sustained winds about 305 miles west of Honolulu, moving westward away from the main Hawaiian Islands, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

Severe flash flooding in Kaʻū cut off road access and inundated homes; the County coordinated search-and-rescue in Nāʻālehu and Waiʻōhinu with National Guard high-water vehicles and a US Coast Guard helicopter, transporting rescued residents to Robert N. Herkes Gym in Pāhala and the Public Works base yard.

Lala strengthened to a Category 1 hurricane: NOAA's 11 PM HST advisory reported 75 mph sustained winds and a 988 mb central pressure about 65 miles west of Kailua-Kona, forecasting 4-8 inches of rain (storm-total maximum 30-35 inches over windward Hawaii Island), 1-3 feet of storm surge and life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Hawaii County Mayor C. Kimo Alameda signed an emergency proclamation for Hawaiʻi County, citing forecasts of 74-110 mph winds, 8-12 inches of rain (10-15 inches over windward areas), 1-3 feet of storm surge and 15-20 foot surf.

Governor Josh Green signed a statewide emergency proclamation ahead of the storm, mobilizing state agencies; about 180 Hawaiʻi National Guard personnel were subsequently positioned statewide, and Hilo and Kona airports and Hawaiʻi Island and Maui County commercial ports were closed as Lala approached.
